title: India's Housing Market Just Had Its Best Quarter in Years. NRI Buyers Are Leading the Luxury Charge.
excerpt: Sales surged 19% across India's top nine cities in Q2 2026, with Bengaluru and Hyderabad leading the boom — and overseas Indians are driving the high-end segment that's propping up the entire market.
body:
India's residential real estate market just posted numbers that would have been unthinkable five years ago. Housing sales across the country's top nine cities surged 19 percent year-on-year to 1,12,458 units in the April–June quarter of 2026, according to PropEquity, even as geopolitical turmoil in the Gulf and global economic jitters kept investors on edge elsewhere.

More striking still: new housing supply jumped 43 percent in the same period, to 1,17,609 units. Developers are not just responding to demand — they are betting that the market has structurally shifted, with southern Indian cities and the luxury segment driving most of the momentum.

Bengaluru and Hyderabad Are India's New Property Powerhouses

The south is running away with the market. Bengaluru recorded 21,516 units sold — a 47 percent leap from a year earlier — cementing its position as India's largest residential market by volume. Hyderabad followed closely, posting sales of 14,410 units (up 22 percent), while Chennai added 6,323 units, an 18 percent increase.

On the supply side, the numbers are even more dramatic. Bengaluru saw 24,340 new units launched (up 71 percent year-on-year), and Hyderabad's launches surged 75 percent to 18,407 units, overtaking Pune, Thane, and Delhi-NCR to become the country's second-largest supply market behind Bengaluru.

![Bengaluru — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/cd/View_from_Visvesvaraya_Industrial_and_Technological_Museum_%282025%29_02.jpg/3840px-View_from_Visvesvaraya_Industrial_and_Technological_Museum_%282025%29_02.jpg)

> **""Southern markets continue to lead growth, while Mumbai and Navi Mumbai have also seen strong demand."

Mumbai Metropolitan Region Roars Back

The western corridor is not standing still."**

"Indian housing market has remained resilient despite the geopolitical uncertainties in the Middle East," said Samir Jasuja, founder and CEO of PropEquity. "Southern markets continue to lead growth, while Mumbai and Navi Mumbai have also seen strong demand."

Mumbai Metropolitan Region Roars Back

The western corridor is not standing still. Navi Mumbai emerged as the fastest-growing market nationally, with sales shooting up 61 percent to 11,029 units and new supply more than doubling (up 116 percent). Mumbai city proper saw a 32 percent jump in sales to 10,561 units, and its supply surged 111 percent. Thane and Pune posted more moderate but steady growth, at 10 percent and 9 percent respectively.

Where the Market Is Cooling

Not every city is celebrating. Kolkata registered the sharpest decline, with sales falling 23 percent to just 3,414 units. Delhi-NCR dropped 14 percent to 10,082 units, with new supply also dipping 6 percent. Analysts point to affordability pressures, delayed infrastructure projects, and a pullback in launches after overheated quarters as the primary culprits.

![Chennai — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/3/32/Chennai_Central.jpg)

The Luxury Pivot — And Why NRIs Are Behind It

Behind the headline sales numbers is a structural transformation. Nearly 42 percent of all new housing supply in the first half of FY26 was in the luxury and ultra-luxury segments — homes priced above ₹1.5 crore ($180,000). While overall sales volumes have moderated from their FY24 peak, the *value* of homes sold keeps climbing. ANAROCK estimates total residential sales value will reach a record ₹9.33 lakh crore (roughly $111 billion) in FY26, a 19 percent jump from the previous year.

A significant chunk of this premium demand is coming from overseas Indians. "Over the past three years, the contribution from NRI buyers has increased significantly for us," noted a senior ANAROCK executive in a recent Outlook Money report. Average residential prices have crossed ₹10,000 per square foot for the first time nationally, and the luxury segment is the only category where demand consistently outpaces supply.

For NRIs earning in dollars, pounds, or dirhams, the math is increasingly compelling. The rupee's relative weakness means a ₹2.5 crore apartment in Bengaluru — a city that tops NRI investment preferences at 31 percent — translates to roughly $300,000. That buys about 150 square feet in Manhattan or a studio in central London. Post-RERA transparency has also dramatically reduced the delivery risk that once scared diaspora buyers away from off-plan purchases.

What It Means for Diaspora Buyers

The market's luxury tilt creates both opportunity and urgency. Prices in premium micro-markets are expected to rise 5 to 7 percent annually through 2028, according to a Reuters poll of property analysts. For NRIs considering a property in India — whether as a future retirement home, a place for aging parents, or a pure yield play — the window of relative value is narrowing.

The demand fundamentals remain strong: India's urban population is growing, infrastructure spending is at record levels, and the mortgage market is deepening. But the affordable housing segment is being left behind. Homes priced below ₹1 crore saw demand plunge 31 percent last year, even as luxury sales held firm. India's housing boom is real — it is just not equally distributed.

For the millions of NRIs watching from Silicon Valley, the Gulf, or the City of London, the question is no longer whether Indian real estate is investable. It is whether they can afford to wait.
